beginner: Kale likes rich, loose soil that holds moisture but still drains well. Mix in plenty of compost before planting. It is not fussy and grows in most garden soils, but it does best when the soil is fertile and never bone dry or waterlogged.
seasoned: Kale is forgiving about soil and grows in a wide range of textures, but it performs best in a fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter. Work in compost before planting and keep moisture even; the plant is a leafy heavy feeder whose tenderness and color suffer in soil that either ponds water or dries out hard.

beginner: Kale grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, around 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, keeping the soil closer to neutral helps.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0; kale still does fine across a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band. Holding the soil toward neutral, roughly 6.8 to 7.2, also helps suppress clubroot, a key brassica soil disease, so a grower with clubroot history should lean to the high end.

beginner: Kale needs regular feeding to keep making tender leaves. Give it a feed when you plant it, again about 4 weeks later, and a light feed after each big harvest so it grows fresh leaves. Do not overdo it, since too much fertilizer makes soft growth that bugs love.
seasoned: Kale is a leafy crop that needs steady nitrogen for tender, dark green leaves. Use a starter fertilizer at transplanting, then side-dress with nitrogen about 4 weeks later, and feed again with a light dose of nitrogen after each heavy cutting of leaves to push new growth. Its nutrient demand is moderate rather than extreme, so avoid overdoing nitrogen, which softens growth and draws aphids.

beginner: Time to feed your kale.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your kale with nitrogen.

beginner: Use a nitrogen-rich feed such as blood meal or a balanced vegetable fertilizer.
seasoned: High N for leafy growth; e.g. 21-0-0 side-dress or blood meal. Starter feed at transplant, then a light nitrogen feed after each cutting.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer.
seasoned: Side-dress about half a cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row roughly 4 weeks after transplanting, then a lighter feed after heavy cuttings.

beginner: Kale does well next to aromatic herbs, onions, and quick cool-season crops like lettuce and beets. The main thing is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share its pests and diseases.
seasoned: Most kale companion pairings are traditional rather than research-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents against cabbage pests, and lettuce, spinach, or beets as cool-season interplants that use space and light while kale is small. The well-grounded caution is to separate kale from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cabbage-family pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for kale; their strong smell is said to help confuse and deter cabbage pests.
seasoned: Onions are one of the better-supported brassica companions. Their pungent allium scent helps mask the kale from cabbage-family pests, loopers, cabbageworms, and root maggots, that hunt partly by smell, and extension trial work including onion in a mix with cole crops showed reduced caterpillar damage. Alliums are shallow-rooted and undemanding, so they tuck around kale without competing for much.

beginner: Dill is a classic friend for cabbage-family plants. Its strong smell is said to put off pests, and its flowers bring in helpful insects.
seasoned: Dill works for kale mainly through beneficial insects. Its umbel flowers attract parasitoid wasps and predators like hoverflies and ladybugs that prey on the aphids and cabbage caterpillars kale draws, and extension work pairing aromatic umbels with brassicas has shown reduced caterpillar damage. Let some dill flower for the benefit, and site it nearby rather than crowding the kale.

beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low, so you can tuck it between young kale plants to use the space while the kale fills in.
seasoned: Lettuce and kale interplant well on structure and timing rather than chemistry. Lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick, kale taller and slower, so the lettuce uses the open ground and light between young kale plants and is harvested before the kale spreads. Expect an efficient use of the bed, not pest protection.

beginner: Keep kale away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, collards, and cauliflower. They share the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes problems worse.
seasoned: Planting kale cheek-by-jowl with its brassica relatives, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, collards, Brussels sprouts, concentrates the whole family's shared pests (cabbage worms, loopers, flea beetles, harlequin bugs, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

beginner: You'll see ragged holes eaten in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and little dark droppings. Some caterpillars loop up in the middle as they crawl.
seasoned: Ragged holes chewed through the leaves, with green caterpillars and dark frass on the foliage. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch; diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed.

beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants like kale and chew the leaves, which are the part you eat.
seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Because kale is harvested as leaves, even modest feeding damages the crop.

beginner: Spray a product called Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or pick the caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) or spinosad, which target caterpillars, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down.

beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover right after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs. Clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.
seasoned: Use floating row cover from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

beginner: You'll see clusters of tiny soft insects on the new growth and tucked into the curled leaves, often a waxy gray-green kind. Leaves curl and pucker, and there may be a sticky coating.
seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on growing tips and leaf undersides; the waxy gray-green cabbage aphid is especially troublesome because it lodges in the crinkles and curls of kale leaves and is very hard to wash out at harvest.

beginner: Aphids are tiny insects that suck juice from the plant. They breed fast and hide deep in kale's crinkled leaves, where they are hard to wash out.
seasoned: Several aphid species, notably the cabbage aphid, suck sap from kale; they multiply quickly and their feeding distorts growth and contaminates the harvested leaves.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil, making sure to hit under the leaves and into the crinkles where they hide. Repeat every few days.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water, or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides and the leaf crinkles; repeat every few days. Curly-leaf varieties are hardest to clear, so catch infestations early.

beginner: Welcome helpful bugs like ladybugs and lacewings that eat aphids, don't overdo the nitrogen fertilizer (lush growth attracts them), and check the new growth often.
seasoned: Encourage natural enemies like ladybugs and lacewings, avoid overfeeding nitrogen (which spurs the soft growth aphids favor), and inspect growing tips early so colonies do not lodge in the leaves.

beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts or kills seedlings and scars the leaves of a leaf crop.

beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover.
seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas and are most damaging at the seedling stage; on kale they also leave cosmetic shot-holes in the harvested leaves.

beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle it.
seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover, and spray spinosad or apply kaolin clay if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.

beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
seasoned: Use row cover from sowing or transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, and clean up weedy brassica relatives nearby.

beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It's worst in cool, wet spring soil.
seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet spring soil.

beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool spring weather.
seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed on the roots below, sometimes killing young plants.

beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.

beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Don't plant into cold, soggy soil, and avoid spots where you grew cabbage-family plants last year.
seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It's mostly a warm-region problem and loves kale.
seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region pest that prefers kale, mustard, and collards over other cole crops.

beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants like kale, mustard, and collards, especially in the South.
seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a brassica-specialist stink bug, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes two to four generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.

beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their eggs (little barrel-shaped eggs in rows), and young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull out badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Pyrethrins are permitted in organic production if pressure is severe.

beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard or an early kale planting to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard, kale, or rapeseed to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots.

beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and causes the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years and spreads in contaminated soil and water.

beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Adding lime to make the soil less acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward 7.0 or above with lime can suppress the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.

beginner: Don't grow kale or its cabbage-family relatives in the same spot more than once every 3 years, or longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
seasoned: Rotate brassicas on a cycle of at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is known; keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot the leaves you want to eat.
seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and rot the harvested leaves.

beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the plant's veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.

beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.

beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for good airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, rotate away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves.
seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors and downgrades the leaves.

beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
seasoned: A fungus-like organism that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it. Kale's cool-season window overlaps the weather it likes.

beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.

beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

beginner: Small dark spots on the leaves that grow into round patches with concentric rings, like a tiny target. Bad cases make the leaves yellow and unusable.
seasoned: Small dark lesions enlarge into circular spots with characteristic concentric rings (a target-spot look) and a yellow halo; because the leaves are the crop, even moderate spotting reduces the harvest. Favored by warm, wet conditions.

beginner: A fungus that spreads in warm, wet weather and infects the leaves, leaving target-like spots. It's worse on stressed plants and in crowded, damp plantings.
seasoned: Fungi in the genus Alternaria (with Cercospora causing a similar leaf spot) infect brassica foliage, spreading by spores in wind and splashing water; infected seed, crop debris, and long leaf wetness drive it.

beginner: Remove and destroy badly spotted leaves, improve airflow so leaves dry quickly, and use a copper spray if it spreads. Avoid wetting the leaves when you water.
seasoned: Remove and destroy spotted leaves and debris, improve airflow, avoid overhead watering, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high.

beginner: Start with clean seed, rotate away from brassicas, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and keep plants healthy so they resist infection.
seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed, rotate away from brassicas, space for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris that harbors spores.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week.
seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept even through the season.

beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week.
seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week, a little more in hot, dry spells.

beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp, soft growth; kale dislikes waterlogged soil and can rot at the crown.

beginner: Wilting leaves that turn tough and bitter.
seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and tough, bitter leaves; drought stress hurts leaf quality and invites pests.

beginner: Keep the soil or tray damp while the seeds come up, without letting the surface dry out.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed or tray surface evenly moist through germination; brassica seed is shallow and should not dry mid-emergence.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp as they grow.
seasoned: Grow the seedlings on with steady, even moisture.

beginner: Water evenly as the plant grows its leaves. Steady water makes the leaves tender and mild.
seasoned: Keep even moisture as the plant builds its leafy frame; steady water sets up tender, mild leaves.

beginner: Keep watering evenly while you harvest outer leaves over the weeks. If the plant dries out, the leaves get tough and strong-tasting.
seasoned: Even moisture through the main leaf-production weeks matters most for tender, mild leaves; drought turns them tough and strong-flavored. Pick the outer leaves and keep the plant watered to keep them coming.

beginner: In winter kale needs little watering, and frost makes it sweeter. Do not keep cold soil soggy.
seasoned: In cold weather a hardy kale plant needs little to no supplemental water; frost actually sweetens the leaves. Avoid waterlogging cold soil.

beginner: Keep the water steady so the leaves stay tender, not tough.
seasoned: Even moisture keeps the leaves tender and mild; dry spells make kale tougher and more bitter.

beginner: Water steadily while the plant is making lots of leaves.
seasoned: Even moisture through the main leaf-production weeks matters most for tender, mild leaves.

beginner: You can sow kale seeds right in the garden or start them indoors. For spring, start seeds about a month before planting out, and set plants in the garden a few weeks before your last frost, or just sow seeds once the soil can be worked. For a fall crop, sow in mid to late summer so it is ready before winter. If you grow your own transplants, let them get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.
seasoned: Kale can be direct sown or transplanted. For a spring crop, start seeds indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before set-out and transplant around 4 to 5 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow as soon as the soil is workable; kale tolerates frost. For a fall and overwintering crop, sow in midsummer (often direct in the garden) so plants size up before cold, then harvest through fall and, in milder zones, winter. Harden transplants off over 7 to 10 days.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A light, well-drained commercial potting mix high in organic matter.

beginner: Mix in some compost for a steady supply of nutrients.
seasoned: Blend in compost and a slow-release nitrogen source; container kale still feeds steadily.

beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in heat and water before the mix dries out.

beginner: Feed a bit more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.
seasoned: Container kale needs more frequent feeding than in-ground plants because watering leaches nutrients.

beginner: In mild-winter areas, kale in a pot keeps going through winter; just move it to a sheltered, sunny spot. In cold areas, pull the pot against the house or into an unheated garage during hard freezes, or grow a fast variety and enjoy it before deep winter.
seasoned: Kale is cold-hardy enough to overwinter in a container in mild zones, where it keeps producing through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot. In colder zones the limited root volume of a pot freezes harder than open ground, so move containers against a wall or into an unheated structure during hard freezes, or treat the potted crop as a single fall-into-early-winter planting.

beginner: Kale grows well in a pot of at least 3 gallons that is 10 inches or more deep, one or two plants per pot. Keep it watered and fed, and pick the outer leaves as you need them. In hot areas, give it some afternoon shade.
seasoned: Kale is a good container crop because it is compact and harvested as leaves over a long period. Use a container of at least 3 gallons and 10 inches deep, one or two plants per pot, and keep moisture even since pots dry quickly. Pick outer leaves and leave the growing point, and in warm regions give afternoon shade and avoid heat-absorbing dark pots.

beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps kale leaves tender.
seasoned: A self-watering container suits kale well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and mild.

beginner: Kale does not get huge, but it grows for a long time, so give it a pot that holds at least 3 gallons and is about 10 inches deep. A wider pot is better than a tall skinny one because it holds moisture better and gives the roots room.
seasoned: Kale stays relatively compact but builds a substantial root system over a long season, so choose a container at least 3 gallons and 10 inches deep. Width matters more than height: a broad pot gives room to grow one or two plants and buffers the fast drying that narrow pots suffer.

beginner: Winterbor and Dwarf Siberian are easy, very hardy choices, great for a fall or winter crop. Red Russian is tender and fast, nice for salads. Lacinato (Dinosaur kale) is popular for cooking but is the least cold-hardy, so cover it when it gets really cold.
seasoned: Match the variety to the slot and the climate. For fall and overwintering, lean on the hardiest types: Winterbor, Improved Dwarf Siberian, and Red Russian shrug off hard frost, while Lacinato is the least cold-hardy and wants protection. Curly types (Winterbor, Vates, Redbor) hold texture and color in cold; flat types (Lacinato, Red Russian) are more tender for fresh eating. Where clubroot or other brassica diseases are a concern, look for resistant cultivars.

beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, collards, and turnips.
seasoned: Other brassicas (broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, collards, Brussels sprouts, kohlrabi, turnip, radish, mustard), which share clubroot and cabbage-family pests.

beginner: Do not plant kale or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting at least 3 years between them, and longer if you have had clubroot, helps avoid soil diseases.
seasoned: Rotate so kale and its brassica relatives do not return to the same ground for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is present, since the clubroot organism persists in soil for years. The University of Minnesota advises not growing cole crops in the same spot for the past four years. Keeping soil pH near neutral also helps suppress clubroot.

beginner: Do not leave kale out on the counter. It wilts and yellows fast in the warmth, so get it into the fridge soon after picking.
seasoned: Kale wilts and toughens at room temperature and its leaves yellow within a day or two, so do not leave it out. Refrigerate as soon as possible after cutting; if it must sit out briefly, stand the stems in water like cut flowers.

beginner: Store kale unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge's crisper drawer, where it stays good for about a week, sometimes up to 2 weeks if very cold. Wait to wash it until you are ready to cook.
seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the crisper; kale holds its quality for roughly 1 week, and up to about 2 weeks held near 32°F at high humidity. Washing before storage traps moisture and speeds spoilage.

beginner: Kale freezes well if you blanch it first. Strip the leaves off the stems, boil them for 2 to 3 minutes, cool them right away in ice water, drain, and freeze.
seasoned: Kale freezes well once blanched: strip the leaves from the stems, blanch about 2 to 3 minutes in boiling water, cool quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. Blanching halts the enzymes that otherwise cause off-flavors and loss of color in storage.

beginner: Kale is best right after you pick it, and the plant is its own best storage: in cool weather the leaves keep on the plant for weeks and even get sweeter after frost. So pick what you need when you need it, and chill it quickly after cutting.
seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden, and a key kale advantage is that the plant itself is the best storage: leaves keep on the plant for weeks in cool weather and sweeten after frost, so harvest close to when you will use it rather than stockpiling. Chilling promptly after cutting keeps the leaves crisp and mild.

beginner: In about 5 to 10 days, your seeds sprout and push up their first two little leaves (the seed leaves).
seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days at soil temperatures of roughly 45 to 85°F, pushing up two seed leaves (cotyledons).

beginner: Keep the soil damp. Once the first real kale leaves appear after the seed leaves, thin crowded seedlings.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed or starting mix evenly moist; thin or pot up once the first true leaves appear.

beginner: Have your seeds come up yet?
seasoned: Did your kale seeds sprout?

beginner: The seedlings grow their real, slightly frilly leaves and a stronger stem. They are ready to move outside at about 4 to 5 weeks old.
seasoned: Young plants develop true leaves and a sturdy stem; kale transplants are ready at about 4 to 5 weeks. Flea beetles are the main seedling threat.

beginner: If you grew transplants, harden them off over about a week before planting out. Watch for flea beetle shot-holes on the young leaves.
seasoned: Harden off over 7 to 10 days before setting out; protect seedlings from flea beetles with row cover.

beginner: How many real leaves do your seedlings have?
seasoned: How many true leaves does your seedling have?

beginner: The plant grows into an upright rosette of big leaves. This is when it builds the frame that you will harvest from for months.
seasoned: The plant builds an upright rosette of large leaves over several weeks, laying down the productive frame.

beginner: Feed with nitrogen and keep it evenly watered so the leaves stay tender. Check for aphids in the leaf crinkles and caterpillars on the undersides.
seasoned: Side-dress with nitrogen, keep moisture even for tender leaves, and scout for aphids and cabbageworms while the frame fills out.

beginner: Is your plant growing lots of healthy leaves?
seasoned: Is your kale putting on healthy leafy growth?

beginner: Once the outer leaves are about hand-sized, start picking. Take the lowest, outside leaves and leave the center to keep growing, so the plant gives leaves for months.
seasoned: Outer leaves reach usable size at about 50 to 65 days (baby leaf around 25 to 30 days); harvest cut-and-come-again, taking the lowest leaves and leaving the growing point.

beginner: Pick the outer leaves regularly, never stripping more than about a third at once. Feed lightly after a big harvest. The leaves taste sweeter after frost.
seasoned: Crop the outer leaves regularly to keep new growth coming, side-dress lightly after heavy picking, and expect the best flavor after a frost.

beginner: Have you started picking outer leaves?
seasoned: Are you harvesting outer leaves?

beginner: As cold sets in, kale keeps going. In mild areas you harvest right through winter; in cold areas the plant may rest under snow or cover and may regrow, then send up a flower stalk (bolt) in spring.
seasoned: Kale is among the hardiest garden vegetables: mature plants tolerate hard frost and into the low-to-mid 20s°F, sweetening as starch converts to sugar. In mild zones it crops through winter; in cold zones it overwinters under cover and resumes, then bolts as spring warms and days lengthen.

beginner: In mild zones, keep picking through winter. In cold zones, protect plants with a row cover or low tunnel. When spring warmth makes the plant bolt, harvest what is left, since the leaves turn bitter once it flowers.
seasoned: Harvest through winter in mild zones; use row cover or low tunnels in cold zones. Once the plant bolts in spring, harvest remaining leaves promptly, as flavor turns bitter, and pull it to make room.

beginner: Is your kale still producing in the cold?
seasoned: Is your kale overwintering or starting to bolt?

beginner: Time to start picking kale leaves
seasoned: Start cropping the outer leaves

beginner: Your kale's outside leaves should be big enough to pick. Take the lowest, outer ones and leave the middle growing, so it keeps making more.
seasoned: Your kale's outer leaves should be about hand-sized now. Begin cropping the lowest, outermost leaves and leave the central growing point so the plant keeps producing for months.

beginner: Time to feed your kale

seasoned: Plants were stunted and chlorotic, wilted by day, and showed galled, clubbed roots, the signature of clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae). seasoned: Kale is a hardy, non-heading cole crop grown for its nutritious leaves, which are harvested continuously rather than as a single head. In mild-winter regions it grows right through winter, and in colder zones it overwinters with simple protection, making it one of the longest-cropping plants a gardener can grow.
